scenarios.title: Distributed API Rate Limiter
scenarios.problem_statement: Design a high-throughput, low-latency distributed rate limiter service to protect our core API gateway from traffic spikes, denial-of-service attempts, and abusive tenants across multi-region clusters.
functional_requirements: Limit requests per client IP, user ID, or API key within configurable time windows (e.g. 100 req/minute).
Return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with informative retry headers when limits are breached.
Support multi-tiered rate limiting rules (tiered subscriptions, burst capacity allowances).
non_functional_requirements: Ultra-low latency overhead (< 5ms p99 at API gateway).
High availability and fault tolerance (soft fail-open if rate limiter cluster fails).
Horizontal scalability supporting millions of active concurrent tokens across multiple regions.

requirements: What criteria will you use to identify and segment clients (IP, API token, user ID)?
What should happen when the rate limiter is unavailable or slow—fail open or fail closed?
high_level_design: Where in the request pipeline would you place the rate limiter—at the API Gateway, sidecar, or reverse proxy?
What data store and algorithmic pattern (Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Sliding Window Log, Sliding Window Counter) would you pick?
deep_dive: How do you handle race conditions when concurrent requests from the same user hit different gateway instances simultaneously?
How would you structure your Redis or in-memory key format and expiration policies to minimize memory footprint?
bottlenecks_tradeoffs: How does your system synchronize state across multiple geographical data centers without incurring cross-region latency?
What monitoring metrics and alert thresholds would you instrument to detect throttling anomalies?

requirements.communication: Clarifies scale (QPS, concurrent users), failure modes (fail-open vs fail-closed), and tenant granularity.
requirements.edge_cases: Identifies distributed clock drift, NAT IP collision, and unauthenticated traffic.

high_level_design.architecture: Positions rate limiter at API Gateway or reverse proxy, justifies caching layer (Redis / Memcached).
high_level_design.data_modeling: Selects appropriate algorithm (e.g. Token Bucket vs Sliding Window Counter) with clear memory usage analysis.

deep_dive.scalability: Resolves distributed concurrency using Lua scripts, Redis pipeline, or local sliding window caches with background sync.
deep_dive.architecture: Defines atomic increment operations and compact byte-level key structures.

bottlenecks_tradeoffs.scalability: Evaluates eventual consistency vs synchronous replication across data centers.
bottlenecks_tradeoffs.edge_cases: Explains grace periods, client retry exponential backoff (Jitter), and circuit breaking.

scenarios.title: Scalable URL Shortener (TinyURL)
scenarios.problem_statement: Design a globally distributed URL shortening service capable of creating compact aliases for long web URLs, redirecting millions of redirect requests with single-digit millisecond latency, and tracking analytics.
functional_requirements: Given a long URL, generate a unique 7-character short URL alias.
Given a short alias, redirect the user via HTTP 301/302 to the original destination with minimal latency.
Support custom short links and optional TTL link expiration.
non_functional_requirements: Massive read-to-write skew (e.g. 100:1 read to write ratio).
High availability (99.99%) and durable persistent storage for billions of URL records.

requirements: What is the expected read-to-write ratio and monthly URL creation volume?
Should redirections use HTTP 301 (Permanent) or HTTP 302 (Temporary), and what are the trade-offs for analytics?
high_level_design: How do you generate unique short aliases (Base62 encoding of counter vs MD5/SHA256 hashing vs Token Generator Service)?
What database technology (NoSQL key-value vs Relational) best accommodates high write throughput and simple key lookups?
deep_dive: How would you architect the Key Generation Service (KGS) to prevent duplicate keys across distributed worker nodes?
How do you leverage caching (Redis, CDN) to handle popular viral links without overwhelming the database?
bottlenecks_tradeoffs: How do you purge or archive expired URLs without causing table locking or database latency spikes?
How would you prevent single points of failure in the Key Generation Service?

requirements.communication: Proactively probes traffic volume, URL character length, alphabet (Base62), and TTL expectations.
requirements.edge_cases: Considers link hijacking, malicious URL spam, and duplicate submissions of the same long URL.

high_level_design.architecture: Chooses between 301 (browser caching saves server load) and 302 (server-side analytics tracking).
high_level_design.data_modeling: Designs lightweight schema (short_key, original_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at) with indexed short_key.

deep_dive.scalability: Designs pre-generated key tokens (KGS) or SnowFlake ID generator; instruments multi-layer caching (LRU cache, Redis).
deep_dive.architecture: Calculates storage requirements accurately for 5-10 year operational horizon.

bottlenecks_tradeoffs.scalability: Explains database partitioning/sharding strategies (hash-based sharding on short_key).
bottlenecks_tradeoffs.edge_cases: Designs lazy-deletion TTL reaper mechanisms to prevent database degradation.

scenarios.title: Real-Time Multi-Channel Notification Platform
scenarios.problem_statement: Design an enterprise-scale notification platform capable of ingesting, prioritizing, and dispatching billions of push notifications, SMS texts, and transactional emails with rate throttling and user preference controls.
functional_requirements: Ingest event notifications from multiple backend microservices via asynchronous API / message queue.
Dispatch notifications across three distinct channels: Mobile Push (APNs/FCM), SMS (Twilio), and Email (SendGrid).
Enforce user opt-out preferences, quiet hours, and frequency deduplication.
non_functional_requirements: High throughput (100,000+ notifications per second during peak breaking news / flash sales).
At-least-once delivery guarantee with idempotency to prevent duplicate messages.
Strict latency tiers (critical OTP security alerts in < 2s; marketing updates in < 15m).

requirements: What are the latency expectations for transactional OTPs versus bulk marketing notifications?
How do you handle third-party provider rate limits or service outages?
high_level_design: How do you decouple ingestion from delivery using distributed message queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS)?
How is user preference and device token state queried and cached without creating an ingestion bottleneck?
deep_dive: How do you guarantee idempotency so a user is not double-billed or sent duplicate SMS notifications on retry?
How would you implement priority queueing so OTP codes bypass queued promotional email batches?
bottlenecks_tradeoffs: What happens when third-party gateways (e.g. APNs or Twilio) throttle requests or experience an outage?
How do you handle dead-letter queues (DLQ) and replay mechanisms for transient downstream failures?

requirements.communication: Distinguishes high-priority transactional alerts from bulk asynchronous campaigns.
requirements.edge_cases: Identifies invalid device tokens, provider-side throttling, and time-zone quiet hour constraints.

high_level_design.architecture: Utilizes partitioned message broker (Kafka/RabbitMQ) with dedicated consumer worker pools per channel.
high_level_design.data_modeling: Models notification templates, recipient preference state, and delivery log schemas with idempotency keys.

deep_dive.scalability: Implements separate priority queues or dedicated topic partitions for low-latency alerts.
deep_dive.architecture: Employs distributed idempotency cache (Redis SETNX on message_id) to eliminate duplicate sends.

bottlenecks_tradeoffs.scalability: Incorporates circuit breakers and backoff retry queues for failing downstream providers.
bottlenecks_tradeoffs.edge_cases: Designs Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ) with alert monitoring and administrative replay capabilities.
